questions.question: Which statement best describes sensory and cognitive development around birth?
options: Birth changes the environment, but development has already begun before birth and continues afterward
Birth marks the point when sensory development begins for the first time
Prenatal life supports motor growth, while learning begins only after delivery
Sensory systems are fully mature before birth and change little afterward
questions.feedback: Birth is a major transition, but sensory and cognitive development begins prenatally and continues after birth.

questions.question: How can researchers infer fetal perception?
options: By asking the mother to describe what she thinks the fetus perceived during stimulation
By measuring stimulus-related changes in behavior, physiology, or brain activity
By measuring only maternal behavior during stimulation
By assuming that any fetal movement reflects conscious perception
questions.feedback: Fetal perception is inferred from controlled changes in fetal behavior, physiology, or neural activity.

questions.question: Which method can directly measure prenatal brain responses?
options: Postnatal EEG recorded several days after birth
Maternal heart-rate recording alone
Fetal MEG or fetal fMRI
Observation of maternal facial expressions
questions.feedback: Fetal MEG, fetal fMRI, and sensory-evoked responses can be used to study prenatal brain activity.

questions.question: Which sensory system becomes functional particularly early in prenatal development?
options: Patterned color vision through the uterine wall
Speech comprehension
Stereoscopic depth perception
Somatosensation and touch
questions.feedback: Somatosensation is presented as one of the earliest sensory systems to become functional.

questions.question: What happens to fetal tactile responses as development proceeds?
options: Responses spread from restricted body regions as somatosensory systems mature
Responses become restricted to the hands as other body regions gradually lose sensitivity
Responses remain unchanged from early gestation until birth
Responses are replaced completely by auditory reactions
questions.feedback: Tactile responsiveness begins in restricted regions and spreads as peripheral and central somatosensory systems mature.

questions.question: Which behavior is already common by the second trimester?
options: Reading visual patterns through the uterine wall
Self-touch and hand-to-face movements
Producing meaningful spoken syllables
Using stereoscopic vision to guide reaching
questions.feedback: By the second trimester, fetuses show self-touch, contact with the uterine wall, hand-to-face movements, and responses to mechanical stimulation.

questions.question: What do studies of fetal hand-to-mouth movements suggest after about 32 weeks?
options: Hand movements become progressively less organized as the fetus approaches the end of gestation
The fetus stops moving the mouth during self-touch
Some movements become anticipatory, with mouth movements beginning before hand contact
Anticipatory behavior appears only after birth
questions.feedback: Increasingly anticipatory sensorimotor organization can be observed from around 32 weeks.

questions.question: How was fetal response to maternal abdominal touch studied?
options: With postnatal observation of infant reaching only
By asking mothers to report whether they felt more fetal movement while the abdomen was touched
With visual stimulation delivered directly to the fetal retina
With maternal abdominal stimulation while fetal movements were monitored using 4D ultrasound
questions.feedback: Maternal abdominal touch was paired with 4D ultrasound measurement of fetal movements.

questions.question: Why are taste and smell closely linked in prenatal life?
options: The fetus swallows amniotic fluid containing changing chemical compounds
Outside air enters the fetal nasal cavity and directly stimulates smell receptors
Chemical signals reach the fetus only through maternal blood and bypass amniotic fluid
Taste buds remain inactive until birth
questions.feedback: Amniotic fluid carries chemical compounds from maternal diet, metabolism, and the fetal environment.

questions.question: What can maternal diet change in the fetal environment?
options: The number of fetal chromosomes
The chemical composition of amniotic fluid
The position of the fetal visual cortex
The basic sequence of fetal DNA
questions.feedback: Chemical compounds related to maternal diet can enter amniotic fluid and contribute to fetal chemosensory experience.

questions.question: In the fetal flavor-discrimination experiment, when were fetuses tested?
options: Only during the first trimester before sensory systems become functional
Only after birth when infants could directly taste the same flavors
At 32 to 36 weeks of gestation
At exactly 20 weeks of gestation
questions.feedback: The study tested fetuses at 32-36 weeks of gestation.

questions.question: How were flavors presented in the fetal flavor-discrimination study?
options: Researchers injected carrot and kale extracts directly into amniotic fluid while imaging fetal movement
Infants received flavored cereal after birth and were later compared with an untreated control group
Flavored objects were placed beside the abdomen
Mothers consumed carrot, kale, or control capsules before 4D ultrasound recording
questions.feedback: Mothers consumed carrot, kale, or control capsules, and fetal facial movements were recorded about 20 minutes later.

questions.question: What facial pattern increased after prenatal carrot exposure?
options: Movements contributing to a laughter-face gestalt
Movements contributing mainly to a cry-face gestalt
A complete absence of measurable facial movement
Only eye closure without other facial changes
questions.feedback: Carrot exposure increased movements contributing to the laughter-face pattern.

questions.question: What facial pattern increased after prenatal kale exposure?
options: Movements contributing mainly to a laughter-face gestalt
Movements contributing to a cry-face gestalt
Only swallowing movements without facial changes
A complete suppression of fetal movement
questions.feedback: Kale exposure increased movements contributing to the cry-face pattern.

questions.question: What is the strongest conclusion from the carrot-versus-kale fetal study?
options: Carrot flavor causes a conscious positive emotional state that can be measured before birth
Kale exposure permanently determines later food preferences and emotional reactions after birth
Late-gestation fetuses can discriminate chemosensory information associated with different flavors
Flavor discrimination begins only after birth
questions.feedback: The study supports fetal discrimination of chemosensory information, not adult-like emotional interpretations of facial patterns.

questions.question: Why should the labels 'laughter-face' and 'cry-face' be interpreted cautiously?
options: The labels refer to maternal facial expressions recorded while mothers consumed carrot or kale capsules
The labels summarize changes in fetal heart rate rather than combinations of facial movements
They prove that the fetus experiences no emotion
They describe facial movement patterns rather than proven conscious emotional states
questions.feedback: The labels describe configurations of facial movements and do not demonstrate conscious happiness or disgust.

questions.question: What do newborn responses to amniotic-fluid odor suggest?
options: Prenatal chemosensory information can be encoded and recognized after birth
Newborn odor preference is created only after the first breastfeeding experience following delivery
The fetus is unable to detect chemical information in amniotic fluid before birth
Amniotic-fluid odors are identical across pregnancies
questions.feedback: Preference for the odor of one's own amniotic fluid supports prenatal detection, encoding, and later recognition.

questions.question: How can prenatal chemosensory learning create continuity across birth?
options: The entire sensory environment remains essentially unchanged across birth, so no transition is required
Some familiar odor and flavor compounds persist in breast-related postnatal environments
Vision replaces chemosensation immediately after delivery and becomes the main familiar cue
All prenatal chemical signals disappear at birth
questions.feedback: Some compounds encountered in amniotic fluid can also be present around the breast and in breast milk.

questions.question: Which sounds contribute to the fetal acoustic environment?
options: Only sounds generated by the fetal nervous system and fetal movements inside the uterus
Only external high-frequency sounds that pass through maternal tissues without being attenuated
Maternal bodily sounds, the mother's voice, and external environmental sounds
Only the maternal heartbeat is audible
questions.feedback: The womb contains maternal heartbeat and respiration, movement and digestive sounds, maternal voice, and external sounds.

questions.question: How do maternal tissues and amniotic fluid modify external sounds?
options: They amplify high frequencies while selectively removing slow temporal changes in the acoustic signal
They block all external speech but preserve every internal maternal sound without alteration
They preserve pitch but eliminate timing
They attenuate higher frequencies while preserving useful temporal and prosodic information
questions.feedback: Prenatal transmission attenuates higher frequencies, but temporal and prosodic information can still reach the fetus.

questions.question: What can acoustic stimulation change during the second half of gestation?
options: Fetal heart rate, body movement, and brain responses
Only maternal blood pressure and respiration change during fetal acoustic stimulation
Only fetal skin pigmentation changes as gestation progresses during repeated sound exposure
Only the position of the placenta changes in response to repeated external sounds
questions.feedback: Acoustic stimulation can evoke measurable changes in fetal heart rate, movement, and neural responses.

questions.question: How do fetal auditory responses change with maturation?
options: Auditory responses become progressively slower and less reliable as the fetus matures
They become faster and more reliable
They disappear during the third trimester despite continued exposure to environmental sounds
They become independent of acoustic stimulation once the auditory system begins functioning
questions.feedback: Auditory responses become faster and more reliable as gestation progresses.

questions.question: Why is the maternal voice a particularly important prenatal stimulus?
options: It is the only sound capable of entering the uterus
It bypasses the fetal auditory system and directly activates cortex
It reaches the fetus through air conduction and vibrations through the mother's body
It reaches the fetus only during maternal sleep
questions.feedback: The maternal voice reaches the fetus through both external sound transmission and body-conducted vibrations.

questions.question: What does newborn preference for the maternal voice indicate?
options: Voice recognition develops only after several months of postnatal exposure to speech
Newborns respond equally to the maternal voice and every unfamiliar female voice
The fetal auditory system remains inactive until the moment of birth
Experience with the mother's voice begins before birth
questions.feedback: A preference present immediately after birth supports prenatal learning of the maternal voice.

questions.question: Which behavioral method can assess newborn preference for the maternal voice?
options: Using newborn behavior including non-nutritive sucking
Using maternal questionnaires about which voice the newborn seemed to prefer
Using visual tracking of photographs of the mother and unfamiliar women
Using changes in fetal eye movements measured during postnatal auditory testing
questions.feedback: Newborn behavior, including non-nutritive sucking, can be used to compare responses to maternal and unfamiliar voices.

questions.question: How does prenatal vision differ from prenatal hearing and touch?
options: It is the first sensory system to become fully mature
It receives much less structured natural stimulation in utero
It receives richer patterned stimulation than hearing
It develops only several years after birth
questions.feedback: Natural intrauterine visual input is weak and poorly structured compared with other prenatal sensory inputs.

questions.question: Can light reach the fetus before birth?
options: No, maternal tissues block every photon throughout pregnancy
Only after the eyes have been exposed to air
Yes, sufficiently intense external light can reach the fetus late in gestation
Only during the first trimester
questions.feedback: Sufficiently intense light can reach the fetus, especially late in gestation.

questions.question: Which measures can reveal fetal responses to external light stimulation?
options: Only changes in maternal pupil diameter while the light is presented through the abdomen
Only maternal verbal reports about whether the fetus seemed to react to the light
Only later language development measured months after the prenatal light stimulation
Heart rate, head or eye movements, and brain activity
questions.feedback: Fetal visual-response studies can measure heart rate, head or eye movements, and neural activity.

questions.question: What should not be concluded from fetal responses to intense light?
options: That prenatal vision is equivalent to normal mature postnatal vision
That the fetal visual system is already capable of responding to sufficiently intense light before birth
That late-gestation fetuses can change head or eye movements after external light stimulation
That sensory responsiveness can emerge before a system provides mature perception of the environment
questions.feedback: Responsiveness to light does not imply mature vision; natural prenatal visual input remains weak and poorly structured.

questions.question: What provides the clearest evidence for simple fetal cognition?
options: Adult-like reasoning can be demonstrated when the fetus changes movement after repeated sensory stimulation
Learning and memory demonstrated through changes in response to experience
Understanding the semantic meaning of spoken language provides the strongest evidence of prenatal cognition
Solving symbolic problems before birth is the clearest demonstration of fetal memory and learning
questions.feedback: Simple learning and memory provide strong evidence for fetal cognitive processing.

questions.question: What is habituation?
options: A stronger response to every repetition of a familiar stimulus
A permanent loss of the ability to detect sensory input
A progressive decrease in response when the same stimulus is repeated
A response that occurs only when a completely new stimulus appears
questions.feedback: Habituation is a decline in response across repeated presentations of the same stimulus.

questions.question: Why is fetal habituation considered evidence of learning?
options: The fetus produces exactly the same response on every trial
The stimulus becomes physically weaker on each presentation
The mother learns to predict the experimenter's timing
The response changes as a consequence of previous stimulation
questions.feedback: Habituation indicates that prior stimulation changes the nervous system's subsequent response.

questions.question: What happens during repeated vibroacoustic stimulation in fetal habituation studies?
options: The fetal motor response progressively decreases across repeated presentations
The fetal motor response increases progressively because each repeated stimulus becomes more salient
The fetus stops responding before the first stimulus is presented and remains inactive afterward
Only maternal movement changes across trials while fetal behavior remains constant throughout stimulation
questions.feedback: A progressive reduction in fetal motor response is consistent with habituation.

questions.question: How does fetal habituation change with gestational age?
options: Older fetuses lose the ability to habituate
Older fetuses generally habituate more efficiently and retain information longer
Habituation is equally efficient at every gestational age
Only younger fetuses can retain information across time
questions.feedback: Older fetuses show more consistent responses, more efficient habituation, and longer retention.

questions.question: What does recognition or retention test in prenatal cognition?
options: Whether the fetus can produce spoken words after hearing the same sound repeatedly
Whether visual acuity reaches an adult-like level before the end of gestation
Whether previous exposure changes a response after some delay
Whether maternal hormone concentrations remain constant during repeated sensory stimulation across time
questions.feedback: Recognition and retention ask whether earlier exposure influences a later response.

questions.question: Why can newborn behavior provide evidence for prenatal memory?
options: Newborn behavior is completely independent of prenatal experience
All newborn preferences are genetically fixed and cannot reflect learning
Prenatal memories can be measured only through maternal reports
Some preferences appear immediately after birth, before extensive postnatal experience
questions.feedback: Immediate newborn preferences can reveal information learned prenatally because little postnatal experience has occurred.

questions.question: Which newborn preference can reflect prenatal sensory experience?
options: Preference for the maternal voice
Preference for written words
Preference for complex geometric proofs
Preference for adult stereoscopic scenes
questions.feedback: Maternal voice, language rhythm, previously heard speech, odors, and flavors can all reflect prenatal familiarity.

questions.question: What is one function of prenatal learning?
options: It produces fully mature adult cognition before delivery
It can make biologically important stimuli familiar before birth
It eliminates the need for postnatal learning
It makes every sensory system equally mature at birth
questions.feedback: Prenatal learning can familiarize the fetus with biologically relevant regularities such as maternal voice, odors, and flavors.

questions.question: Which statement best describes the relation between prenatal learning and adult cognition?
options: Prenatal learning demonstrates mature language comprehension
Prenatal learning proves adult-like conscious reasoning
Prenatal learning reflects basic discrimination, learning, and memory rather than adult-like thought
Prenatal learning means cognitive development is complete before birth
questions.feedback: Basic fetal learning and memory should be distinguished from adult-like thought, language, or conscious understanding.

questions.question: What is the overall conclusion about fetal sensory and cognitive function?
options: The fetus is sensory inactive until delivery
Only motor development occurs before birth
All mature cognitive abilities are already present prenatally
The fetus can detect, discriminate, learn, and retain some information before birth
questions.feedback: Human fetuses can detect sensory information, discriminate some properties, habituate, learn recurring patterns, and retain information.
